pr_body:
The components E2E tests drifted a bit out of sync with reality, so this gets them back into line.

1. **All quarantined tests dealt with**. There were three categories:
 * Those that have actually always passed since the great E2E reliability push many months ago. These are simply unquarantined.
 * One test that became broken because of a Selenium API change. This is fixed in this PR and unquarantined. Fixes https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/issues/38613.
 * The ignitor tests.
2. **Ignitor and its tests removed**. We've been saying for a while we want to do this, since the behavior is covered sufficiently by the Selenium E2E tests and certain relatively new unit tests, and because we had never managed to make Ignitor truly stable. However nobody was ready to delete them so they got left in a limbo "quarantined" state even though we had no plans to unquarantine them ever, and their results didn't give us any value whether they passed or failed. This PR finally puts them out of their misery.

The net result is that nothing in Components E2E test is quarantined after this. My personal preference would be not to even have a "quarantine" concept in this area, since I find it not to add value and results in us just ignoring problems over a long period. I'm not removing the quarantining support in this PR since it was only added relatively recently, but lets see if we can avoid using it in the coming months!
pr_comments:
> What is your objection to quarantining in this context

It's just that, as far as I'm aware, we're in a position to treat these E2E tests as being reliable. As far as I know the pass rate has been extremely high (maybe even 100%) since the push to improve E2E test reliability. If one of them fails, it's very likely to indicate a real problem such as a product regression or something like the breaking Selenium API change that was fixed in this PR. Quarantining one individual test is more likely to just suppress and ignore a problem that we should be dealing with immediately, and that's exactly what happened in the case of #38613 (it wasn't flaky; it was broken due to an API change).

If the concept of flakiness does come back into the E2E tests, and some specific **test** (not the infrastructure as a whole) is agreed to be flaky then I agree that having a formal process to track that test's reliability over time is valuable. As far as I'm aware we're not in this situation with E2E tests currently but I accept it could happen in the future 😄 

> Why wasn't #33733 every marked as test-fixed❔ Many of these tests would have been unquarantined a while ago if we'd followed the agreed process.

Because nothing specific was done to fix that individual test. The approach to running the E2E tests was changed, and that has resulted in them all becoming reliable. I guess it would have been best if I'd speculatively added `test-fixed` to all the issues relating to E2E tests even before I had confirmation that the runner changes had the desired effect. It was a situation that didn't fit into the process as I understood it, but perhaps I should have understood it differently. I guess at least at the point where I became confident that the new pipeline was good I should have gone and added the `test-fixed` labels.
